## Subscriptions

`Client::subscribe(EventInterest, Arc<dyn EventHandler>)` returns a RAII `Subscription`. `subscribe_handler` samples the handler's interest at registration. Keep the token: dropping it removes future dispatch registrations, while an old dispatch snapshot or accepted callback may still finish. `update_interest` changes future filtering, `unsubscribe` removes explicitly, and `detach` intentionally leaves the registration installed.

`CallbackEventHandler::from_callback(&client, interest, delivery, callback)` builds an async adapter for external subscriptions. Retain its Arc to inspect `EventDeliveryStats`; `cancel()` aborts accepted work. Removing a subscription does not drain the adapter. Idle workers hold `Weak<Client>` and upgrade for callback execution.

`EventKind::ALL` contains every current kind. Iterate that slice or call `.len()` when you need its count. Do not hard-code a kind count or infer names from debug text. Event kinds and serialized event variants are append-only; match extensible enums with fallback arms and build payloads with their supported builders.

## StatusPrivacyUpdate

Carries the synced `StatusPrivacyAction`, timestamp, and `from_full_sync`. `client.status().audience()` reads the observed action or returns `None`. Applications choose recipient lists; this observation does not filter outbound status recipients.

## UnarchiveChatsSettingUpdate

`unarchive_chats` is the inverse of the phone's **Keep chats archived** switch. `true` means a new message can move the chat out of the archive. The payload also carries timestamp, the typed action, and `from_full_sync`; an absent flag does not fabricate a change.

## ReachoutTimelockUpdate

The parsed push uses the same `ReachoutTimelock` state as `mex().fetch_reachout_timelock()`. It precedes its raw MEX twin and retains optional source, stanza ID, and raw backlog marker. `is_active == Some(false)` reports a lifted restriction; `None` does not assert activity. The event does not enforce outgoing-send policy automatically.

## CallLogHistory

Pairing history emits typed call records after the chunk's harvest and legacy `HistorySync` event, in record wire order. `record` remains unmodified. Creator, direction, and start time stay optional when absent, invalid, or unknown; `record.is_incoming` does not invent direction. `sync_type` and `chunk_order` retain history provenance, not app-state full-sync provenance.

Over-budget chunks can suppress typed call events while leaving raw lazy history available. Replay can repeat calls; there is no cross-chunk ordering or dedup guarantee. Upsert using observed call ID and creator when available. `CallLogSync` is the separate app-state mutation event: its timestamp is mutation-write time, not the call's start time.

## Mutation timestamps

Chat-action payloads exposing `action_timestamp: Option<DateTime<Utc>>` distinguish a missing or invalid wire timestamp from a valid Unix-epoch timestamp. The compatibility `timestamp` can contain a fallback. Use the optional observation for ordering decisions instead of treating a fallback as server evidence.

## LabelSublistUpdate

On [main snapshot `35a69a14`](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/blob/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc/wacore/src/types/events.rs), apply `Event::LabelSublistUpdate` idempotently by `(predefined_id, chat_jid)`. `LabelSublistChange::Upsert { sub_list_id }` replaces an entry and `Remove` deletes it. Keep a fallback arm because the change enum is non-exhaustive. Unknown signed numeric IDs are retained; zero is a value, not a removal.

This event does not assign the parent label, reorder lists or describe computed AI handoff filters. The SDK has no sublist membership store and does not synthesize removals from a deleted parent or an omitted snapshot entry. Persist membership in your own store. Preserve `action_timestamp: Option<DateTime<Utc>>` and `from_full_sync` separately; `false` can include recovery/replay and does not certify live traffic.


# Storage
Source: https://whatsapp-rust.jlucaso.com/concepts/storage

Choose a backend and preserve account scope, validated secrets and durable state

<Note>
  Examples on this page target [source snapshot `35a69a14`](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/tree/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc), not a crates.io release. Use the [current API guide](/guides/current-api) to select the matching dependency.
</Note>

## Storage domains

The client coordinates five backend domains through `PersistenceManager`:

| Trait | Responsibility |
| - | - |
| `SignalStore` | Identities, sessions, pre-keys and sender keys |
| `AppSyncStore` | App-state keys, versions and mutation MACs |
| `ProtocolStore` | Protocol metadata, identity mappings and pending inbound replay |
| `MsgSecretStore` | Validated parent message secrets, event times and retention deadlines |
| `DeviceStore` | Account-scoped device state and storage operations |

A type implementing all five automatically implements `Backend`. Do not omit `MsgSecretStore` from a custom adapter.

```mermaid theme={null}
graph TD
    Client --> PersistenceManager
    PersistenceManager --> Backend
    Backend --> SignalStore
    Backend --> AppSyncStore
    Backend --> ProtocolStore
    Backend --> MsgSecretStore
    Backend --> DeviceStore
    SignalStore --> Store
    AppSyncStore --> Store
    ProtocolStore --> Store
    MsgSecretStore --> Store
    DeviceStore --> Store
```

## Select account scope

Use `SqliteStore::open` for the default account or the `SqliteDatabase` facade to provision, select and enumerate accounts. An account store scopes state to its device ID. A database-wide reader or adapter has a different lifetime and scope; do not treat its resource report as an account-only measurement.

Register a concrete backend with the bot/client builder or an existing `Arc<dyn Backend>` with the corresponding `with_backend_arc` method. See [SQLite storage](/api/store#sqlitestore-implementation) and [custom backends](/guides/custom-backends).

## Change device state through the manager

The manager owns mutable device state and publishes a cached immutable snapshot. Reads use the snapshot; updates go through the manager's commands or mutation API so publication, dirty tracking and persistence ordering stay consistent. Directly changing a shared `Device` bypasses those obligations.

The implementation uses portable synchronization. Its internal fields and locks are not a second public storage API. Use the source reference for current details rather than rebuilding the manager from a copied struct definition.

## Validate stored secrets

`get_stored_msg_secret` returns a validated `MessageSecret` and the parent's optional Unix-seconds timestamp. Unknown time is `None`. A malformed persisted byte length is a typed error, not a secret to pad or truncate. The byte-only read is an explicit projection of that validated read.

`expires_at` is an independent retention deadline. A zero expiry means never; upserts keep the later deadline, with never winning. Parent timestamps use the later non-zero value and cannot be replaced by an unknown zero. See [MsgSecretStore](/api/store#msgsecretstore) and [current contracts](/guides/current-api#hooks-and-backend-reads).

## Preserve commit boundaries

Persist Signal changes before sending an envelope that advances their ratchets. An adapter's in-memory cache does not replace that write barrier.

For durable incoming delivery, store pending payloads and implement the protocol-store replay methods. Register an idempotent `InboundDurabilityHook` to commit application data before acknowledgement. Use `(chat, sender, id)` as the identity, since IDs alone can collide across chats or senders. A crash between the application's commit and ACK can replay an already committed message.

Read [inbound durability](/advanced/inbound-durability) for commit order, offline batches, PDO recovery and failure boundaries. On current main, the builder probes bounded exact/group-alias pending reads and conditional replacement/deletion, alongside the pending-store contract. It rejects unsupported adapters with `UnsupportedDurabilityBackend`. See the [ProtocolStore reference](/api/store#pending-inbound-durability-operations) and [bounded backend semantics](/guides/custom-backends#bounded-pending-message-storage). A successful probe does not establish batch atomicity or crash durability.

## Source reference

[Storage traits](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/blob/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc/wacore/src/store/traits.rs) · [PersistenceManager](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/blob/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc/src/store/persistence_manager.rs) · [SQLite adapter](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/blob/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc/storages/sqlite-storage/src/lib.rs)

## Cache coherence

Signal session/sender-key caches buffer mutations for the durable flush boundary. They are distinct from public lookup caches and cannot be discarded as a substitute for committing ratchet state. Fine-grained notification patches keep known cached metadata coherent; unknown entries or unsupported patches may require invalidation and a later fetch. See the source's cache implementation and [state management](/advanced/state-management).

LID/PN mappings preserve both addressing namespaces. Learning a mapping does not make the identities cryptographically interchangeable for an existing poll, event or encrypted add-on. Use the exact recorded creator with a creation reference, and let each facade perform its documented address resolution.

## Tune database resources

Tune `SqliteDatabaseConfig` at database scope. Keep writer `pool_size` at 1 to avoid deferred read-to-write upgrade deadlocks; `busy_timeout` cannot resolve them. Reader connections can increase read concurrency under WAL while consuming their own page-cache resources; adding write concurrency does not make SQLite a multi-writer database. Use the [current SQLite configuration](/api/store#sqlitestore-implementation) and resource reports instead of old per-account pool or thread-count tables.

## Migrate persisted data

Back up the database before an incompatible format migration. Follow the [storage migration reference](/api/store) for supported migrations and legacy session interoperability. Changing a library feature does not retroactively validate arbitrary stored bytes. Do not hand-rewrite Signal sessions or drop account-scoped state to bypass an invalid-data error.


# Community management
Source: https://whatsapp-rust.jlucaso.com/guides/communities

Create a community safely and manage linked subgroups without losing partial failures

<Note>
  Examples on this page target [source snapshot `35a69a14`](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/tree/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc), not a crates.io release. Use the [current API guide](/guides/current-api) to select the matching dependency.
</Note>

## Create once

Build validated `CreateCommunityOptions` and use `result.metadata.id` as the created JID. If optional description configuration fails after creation, handle `ConfigurationFailed` and resume on its `created_jid`. The [community task reference](/api/community#create) includes a complete recovery example.

Creation defaults include a general chat. Change supported options explicitly after construction when your application needs a different policy. Do not recreate an existing parent to repair its description.

## Link groups and inspect every result

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::{Client, Jid};

async fn link(client: &Client, parent: &Jid, children: &[Jid]) -> whatsapp_rust::anyhow::Result<()> {
    let result = client.community().link_subgroups(parent, children).await?;
    for jid in &result.linked_jids {
        println!("linked {jid}");
    }
    for failure in &result.failed_groups {
        eprintln!("{}: {}", failure.jid, failure.code);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

Use `CreateSubgroupOptions` or `LinkSubgroupOptions` with `SubgroupVisibility` when visibility matters. Keep successful and failed entries separate when deciding which ones to retry. Query subgroup pagination and membership approval rather than treating a returned container as a complete joined membership list.

## Address announcement posts

Use an inbound post's `message_ref()` for reactions and comments so its original author and context remain available. A group's visible addressing namespace is not necessarily the creator identity used for encryption. Store the original creator and secret if you need an encrypted edit or a manually reconstructed reference.

`client.comments().send_text(&target, text)` posts a typed comment. For an already captured parent secret, the comments facade also exposes a typed path using the exact creator and secret; consult its source before bypassing store resolution. A new comment gets its own secret so add-ons can address that comment.

For received comments, `InboundMessage::comment_target` identifies the parent post. `InboundMessage::message_ref()` still addresses the comment itself.

## Read metadata and pictures

Use `groups().list_participating` or community overviews for listing. Fetch full metadata only when you need it; use group routing information for encryption fanout. These projections have different network, cache and identity-resolution costs.

Single community parent pictures use `pictures().lookup` with `ProfilePictureTarget::Community`. There is no implicit fallback from the normal group route.

See [community operations](/api/community), [group projections](/api/groups), [pictures](/api/pictures) and [current contracts](/guides/current-api).


# Current API contracts
Source: https://whatsapp-rust.jlucaso.com/guides/current-api

Choose supported requests, message references and storage boundaries

## Select a matching source

These examples use the merged source snapshot [35a69a14](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/tree/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc). The package's declared version does not prove that a main-branch API exists in the published crate. Use the pinned dependency from [installation](/installation) to compile these examples. For a released dependency, select its exact version in [Rustdoc](https://docs.rs/whatsapp-rust).

## Sends and edits

Use `send_text`, `send_message` or `forward_message` for default sends. Use `send(SendRequest::new(chat, message).with_options(options))` for custom options. Build `SendOptions` and `EditOptions` from `Default` with their typed setters.

Pass `EditRequest::new(target, replacement)` to `edit_message`. Encrypted edits carry the original crypto creator and validated secret through `with_secret`. Keep the original target separately from the result's operation ID. See [sending](/api/send).

## Message actions and identity

Obtain `MessageRef` from `InboundMessage`, `MessageContext` or `SendResult`. For stored addressing, validate `MessageRef::new(chat, MessageId, original_sender, from_me)?`. Group and status references retain the original author. Construction validates shape and does not grant server permissions.

Reactions, revokes, pins, keeps, stars and local message deletion take that reference. Message labels take the reference's chat and typed `MessageId`. Build app-state ranges with `message_range(last, system, [(target, timestamp)])`; the helper accepts typed references directly. Channel actions take `NewsletterMessageRef`: edits and revokes require the client `MessageId`; reactions and poll votes require the observed `ServerMessageId`. An outer `StanzaId` identifies the operation for ACK correlation. These IDs have separate purposes.

## Waiters, activity, and media

Keep the `NodeWaiter` returned by `wait_for_node` or `wait_for_sent_node` until completion. Dropping it removes its subscription even without traffic. An active incoming waiter can survive reconnect.

Global availability uses `PresenceStatus`; chat activity uses `ChatActivity` in both outgoing calls and events. See [chatstate](/api/chatstate) and [receipt JSON persistence](/api/receipt#json-persistence).

Reupload requests contain a `MessageRef` and a 32-byte media key. Identical concurrent requests share a recovery; conflicting uses of the same ID return an error. Batch capacity counts distinct operations. Errors retain the failed phase or original rejection response. See [media reupload](/api/media-reupload).

Build stored download metadata with the fallible `DownloadParams::encrypted` or `plaintext` constructor. Fields are private; import `Downloadable` for read access. Download routes contain only hosts. Use `MediaRoute::new(hosts)` or `default_hosts()`. Downloadable values and writers follow platform send bounds. See [download](/api/download).

## Push-name completion

Inspect `PushNameOutcome`: `SyncPending` retains an app-state failure even though presence was sent and the local name updated. Retain the desired name and retry only synchronization with `sync_push_name` when appropriate. See [profile](/api/profile).

## Polls and events

Creation returns `Result<CreatedPoll, PollError>` or `Result<CreatedEvent, SendError>`. Read the send result, creator and secret through named accessors or transfer ownership with `into_parts()`. Persist the original ID, chat addressing, crypto creator and secret together before dropping the creation result if you need later updates.

Use `vote(&PollRef, selected_options)` and `decrypt_vote(ciphertext, &PollRef, voter)` for polls. `decrypt_vote_raw` accepts explicit bytes, original ID and identities at an interop boundary. Event RSVPs use `respond(&EventRef, response, extra_guests)`. A later PN/LID alias does not replace the recorded crypto creator.

Named results redact their debug representation. Exported secret bytes and the nested send protobuf remain sensitive. See [polls](/api/polls) and [events](/api/events).

## Groups and communities

Construct `GroupCreateOptions` with a required subject and `GroupParticipantOptions` with a JID. Build extensible mock outputs with `GroupMetadata::new` and `GroupParticipant::new`; use `..` in DTO patterns and a fallback when matching extensible enums.

Choose overview, full metadata or routing projections according to the task. Preserve found, truncated, forbidden and missing batch outcomes.

`CreateCommunityOptions::new(name)?` validates the subject; descriptions use `GroupDescription`. `ConfigurationFailed` means creation succeeded before follow-up configuration failed. Resume on `created_jid` rather than create a duplicate. Link/unlink failures are `SubgroupFailure` records; subgroup participant counts are `(Jid, u32)` tuples. See [groups](/api/groups) and [communities](/api/community).

## Pictures and status

Use `pictures().lookup(ProfilePictureRequest::new(target, size))` with an explicit contact, group or community target. An `Unchanged` result does not supply a new image, and a 429 remains an operational error with rejection metadata.

Status posts need caller-selected recipients. Synced audience observations do not filter recipients automatically. Build `StatusSendOptions` with typed `MessageId` for content and `StanzaId` for operations; revokes retain the original audience. See [pictures](/api/pictures) and [status](/api/status).

## Hooks and backend reads

A backend implements all five traits: Signal, app state, protocol, message secrets and device storage. The required secret-store methods are `put_msg_secrets`, `get_stored_msg_secret` and `delete_expired_msg_secrets`. The named read returns a validated secret and optional parent timestamp. Unknown time is `None`; it is neither the epoch nor the expiry deadline. Preserve deterministic expiry and timestamp merges on writes. See [storage](/api/store#msgsecretstore).

An inbound durability hook commits idempotently by `(chat, sender, message_id)` before returning success. PDO placeholder recovery is event-only; a later encrypted retry still crosses the durability gate even if its equivalent event was already published. See [inbound durability](/advanced/inbound-durability).

Custom backends must explicitly implement `AppSyncStore::commit_patch` and the two `ProtocolStore` token merges, `touch_tc_token_sender_timestamp` and `store_received_tc_token`. These methods have no sequential defaults. Preserve atomic version/MAC updates and concurrent token fields; batching or flushing alone is insufficient. See [atomic storage operations](/guides/custom-backends#implement-atomic-storage-operations).

## SQLite database and account scope

Use `SqliteStore::open` for the default account. Configure resources with `SqliteDatabaseConfig` when opening `SqliteDatabase`. Select with `store(id)`, provision a chosen unused ID with `provision_device`, or allocate with `create_device`. Enumeration, reset and removal belong to the database facade.

Selection does not create a row. Stop an account's background tasks before reset/removal; retained handles are not revoked. Keep writer `pool_size` at 1 and use `read_pool_size` for eligible concurrent reads. Count database-wide resource reports once per database. See [storage tasks](/api/store).

## Migrating existing integrations

The [migration guide](/guides/rust-api-migration) audits [main `35a69a14`](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/tree/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc). Installation and reference examples use that same revision. Before upgrading, replace generated protobuf literals and exhaustive patterns, implement bounded conditional pending storage for message durability, and register group notification capture independently when you need it. See [protobuf evolution](/api/waproto#source-evolution), [retained plaintext](/advanced/inbound-durability#retained-plaintext-on-current-main), [group capture](/api/groups#durable-notification-capture), and [identity learning](/api/contacts#learning-lid-and-phone-aliases).


# Custom Backends
Source: https://whatsapp-rust.jlucaso.com/guides/custom-backends

Learn how to implement custom storage, transport, and HTTP backends for whatsapp-rust

<Note>
  Examples on this page target [source snapshot `35a69a14`](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/tree/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc), not a crates.io release. Use the [current API guide](/guides/current-api) to select the matching dependency.

  Custom backends must explicitly implement atomic patch commits and token merges. The sections below describe their required semantics.
</Note>

## Overview

This guide covers implementing custom backends for storage, network transport, and HTTP operations in whatsapp-rust. The library uses trait-based abstractions to allow full customization.

## Storage backend architecture

A `Backend` implements five traits: `SignalStore`, `AppSyncStore`, `ProtocolStore`, `MsgSecretStore` and `DeviceStore`. The blanket implementation supplies `Backend` once all five are implemented. A four-trait adapter is incomplete.

Use the pinned trait source for exact required methods and its Rustdoc for default behavior. Your database schema and transaction implementation remain adapter-specific; copying a partial SQL sketch is not a complete backend implementation.

## Implement the secret read boundary

`MsgSecretStore::get_stored_msg_secret(chat, sender, id)` is required. Return a validated secret plus the parent's available timestamp. Do not return an arbitrary byte vector and assume the read is valid.

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::StoredMessageSecret;
use whatsapp_rust::wacore::store::error::Result;

fn read_projection(bytes: &[u8], parent_time: Option<i64>) -> Result<StoredMessageSecret> {
    let stored = StoredMessageSecret::from_stored_bytes(bytes, parent_time.unwrap_or(0))?;
    Ok(stored)
}
```

Return `None` when there is no row. Unknown parent time is explicit `None`; a malformed secret returns `InvalidMessageSecret`. Implement `put_msg_secrets` and `delete_expired_msg_secrets` too. Preserve the expiry and timestamp conflict merge rules documented in [MsgSecretStore](/api/store#msgsecretstore).

## Implement atomic storage operations

Implement these methods explicitly when adopting the merged #1681 contract in a custom Rust backend:

* `ProtocolStore::touch_tc_token_sender_timestamp`
* `ProtocolStore::store_received_tc_token`
* `AppSyncStore::commit_patch`

Their signatures are unchanged, but the sequential default implementations were removed. This is a source compatibility break for adapters that inherited them. Update forwarding wrappers too; delegate the whole operation to the backing store's atomic implementation.

For trusted-contact tokens, make the comparison and update atomic in the account's storage scope. Advancing the sender timestamp preserves the received bytes and timestamp and keeps the maximum sender timestamp. Storing a received token preserves the sender timestamp. Replace a real token only when the incoming timestamp is greater than or equal to the stored timestamp; an empty placeholder must accept the first real token even if that token's timestamp is older.

Use a transaction, a conditional update with CAS retry, or a lock shared by every writer of the same data. A lock on one adapter instance does not coordinate another process or connection. `put_tc_token` remains a full-row replacement; use the field-specific methods for concurrent issuance and reception.

For an app-state patch, atomically store the collection version/hash, remove the listed MACs, then add the supplied MACs. If an index appears in both lists, its added value wins. Scope the entire operation to the account. Errors and cancellation must never leave a new cursor paired with only part of its MAC changes.

A sequence of KV callbacks, a batch without transaction semantics, and a later flush do not satisfy this contract. Do not replace a missing atomic implementation with a no-op or the old read/modify/write default. In-memory storage uses one state lock; SQLite uses a transaction. Neither requires a schema or key-format migration.

Atomicity and durability are separate. SQLite can return a typed `CommitBarrierError` after the entire SQL transaction has committed. Preserve the error and its cause; do not treat it as success or assume it rolled back. The app-state processor publishes a patch's mutations only after `commit_patch` returns `Ok`. Atomicity alone does not recover mutation delivery after a post-commit barrier failure, and retrying the processor does not guarantee replay of that cursor.

## Preserve durability

Signal sessions and sender keys must become durable before publishing messages that advance their ratchets. Backend batching must preserve required ordering; an in-memory cache alone does not provide crash safety.

For crash replay, implement the pending-inbound methods on `ProtocolStore`. Store the pending payload before acknowledgement, and clear it only at the documented commit boundary. The consumer hook still needs idempotent commits by `(chat, sender, id)` because a crash can occur after the application's commit and before the server receives its ACK. See [inbound durability](/advanced/inbound-durability).

Device-scoped operations must isolate one account from another. The scope of `DeviceStore::resource_report` depends on the adapter. SQLite reports the shared database pool through this legacy trait method; count it once per database. Use `SqliteStore::scoped_resource_report()` for an account and `SqliteDatabase::resource_report()` for the database-wide report. Register an owned adapter with `with_backend` or an `Arc<dyn Backend>` with `with_backend_arc`.

[Storage trait reference](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/blob/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc/wacore/src/store/traits.rs) · [SQLite reference implementation](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/blob/35a69a14149fa2cd2a0cc719f875f441d1c6e1dc/storages/sqlite-storage/src/lib.rs)

## Custom Runtime

The `Runtime` trait is the foundation of the runtime-agnostic architecture. It abstracts async task spawning, sleeping, blocking operations, and cooperative yielding. Implement it to use a different async runtime (e.g., async-std, smol, or a WASM executor).

### The Runtime trait

```rust theme={null}
use std::future::Future;
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::time::Duration;
use async_trait::async_trait;
use whatsapp_rust::wacore::runtime::{AbortHandle, Runtime};

pub struct MyRuntime;

#[async_trait]
impl Runtime for MyRuntime {
    fn spawn(
        &self,
        future: Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'static>>,
    ) -> AbortHandle {
        // Spawn a task on your runtime and return an AbortHandle
        // that cancels the task when called
        let handle = my_runtime::spawn(future);
        AbortHandle::new(move || handle.cancel())
    }

    fn sleep(&self, duration: Duration) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send>> {
        // Return a future that completes after the given duration
        Box::pin(my_runtime::sleep(duration))
    }

    fn spawn_blocking(
        &self,
        f: Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>,
    ) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send>> {
        // Offload a blocking closure to a thread pool
        Box::pin(async {
            let _ = my_runtime::spawn_blocking(f).await;
        })
    }

    fn yield_now(&self) -> Option<Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send>>> {
        // Return Some(future) if cooperative yielding is needed,
        // or None if the runtime handles this automatically
        // (e.g., multi-threaded runtimes don't need explicit yielding)
        None
    }

    fn yield_frequency(&self) -> u32 {
        // How many items to process before yielding in tight loops.
        // Default is 10. Single-threaded runtimes should return 1
        // to avoid starving the event loop.
        10
    }
}
```

### AbortHandle

`AbortHandle` is a type-erased cancellation handle marked `#[must_use]`. Dropping an `AbortHandle` requests cancellation of the spawned task without waiting for destruction or cleanup. Call `.detach()` to prevent automatic cancellation for fire-and-forget tasks where the task should run to completion even if the parent scope is dropped.

<Warning>
  Because `AbortHandle` is `#[must_use]`, the compiler warns if you discard the return value of `Runtime::spawn()`. You must either store the handle (to abort later), call `.detach()` (to let the task run freely), or explicitly call `.abort()`.
</Warning>

```rust theme={null}
// Store the handle to abort later
let handle = runtime.spawn(Box::pin(my_task()));
// ...
handle.abort(); // Cancel the task

// Detach for fire-and-forget tasks
runtime.spawn(Box::pin(background_work())).detach();
```

As of [#1124](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust/pull/1124), `Runtime` also has `spawn_detached` for fire-and-forget spawns:

```rust theme={null}
runtime.spawn_detached(Box::pin(background_work()));
```

The trait-level default is exactly `self.spawn(future).detach()` — the same cost as writing both calls out by hand, kept only so existing `Runtime` implementations keep compiling and behaving unchanged. It is **not** itself the optimization: `spawn` still boxes a `dyn FnOnce` capturing the executor's own handle to build the `AbortHandle`, and the default still builds and immediately drops it.

The saving requires overriding `spawn_detached` to bypass `spawn` entirely. The bundled `TokioRuntime` does exactly that in `src/runtime_impl.rs`:

```rust theme={null}
fn spawn_detached(&self, future: Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'static>>) {
    tokio::spawn(future);
}
```

This never constructs an `AbortHandle` at all. Implement `spawn_detached` this way for your own runtime if it can spawn a task with no cancellation bookkeeping; otherwise the inherited default is a correct (if not faster) fallback.

### Using your runtime

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::bot::Bot;

let mut bot = Bot::builder()
    .with_backend(backend)
    .with_transport_factory(transport_factory)
    .with_http_client(http_client)
    .with_runtime(MyRuntime)
    .build()
    .await?;
```

<Tip>
  To target WASM, disable all default features and implement `Runtime` without `Send` bounds. On `target_arch = "wasm32"`, the trait automatically removes `Send` requirements.
</Tip>

<Note>
  **`Spawnable` trait (v0.6).** The future-bound that generic spawn helpers use is now the `Spawnable` marker trait instead of a hardcoded `Send + 'static`. On native targets `Spawnable = Send + 'static`; on `wasm32` it's just `'static` (WASM runtimes are single-threaded and can't require `Send`). `Runtime::spawn`'s signature is unchanged — this only matters if you write your own generic helpers over spawnable futures, in which case bound them on `wacore::runtime::Spawnable` rather than `Send + 'static` so they compile on both targets.
</Note>

<Note>
  If you are implementing a single-threaded runtime, override `yield_frequency()` to return `1` and have `yield_now()` return `Some(future)`. This ensures the event loop is not starved during tight processing loops (e.g., decoding incoming frames).
</Note>

## Proxy and custom TLS

whatsapp-rust has two separate network layers, each with its own extension point for proxy and TLS customization:

| Layer | Purpose | Extension point |
| - | - | - |
| **WebSocket transport** | WhatsApp protocol connection | `TransportFactory` trait / `with_connector` |
| **HTTP client** | Media upload/download, version fetching | `HttpClient` trait / `UreqHttpClient::with_agent` |

To route all traffic through a proxy, you need to configure **both** layers.

### Custom TLS for the WebSocket transport

Use `TokioWebSocketTransportFactory::with_connector` to supply a custom TLS `Connector` — for example, adding custom CA certificates or client certificates:

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust_tokio_transport::{TokioWebSocketTransportFactory, Connector};
use tokio_rustls::TlsConnector;
use rustls::RootCertStore;
use std::sync::Arc;

let mut root_store = RootCertStore::empty();
root_store.add_parsable_certificates(my_ca_certs);

let tls_config = rustls::ClientConfig::builder()
    .with_root_certificates(root_store)
    .with_no_client_auth();

let connector = Connector::Rustls(TlsConnector::from(Arc::new(tls_config)));

let factory = TokioWebSocketTransportFactory::new()
    .with_connector(connector);
```

Use `default_tls_connector()` to inspect or replicate the default TLS configuration as a starting point.

### Custom Origin for a relay

`TokioWebSocketTransportFactory` sends `Origin: https://web.whatsapp.com` on every upgrade by default, matching what whatsmeow and Baileys send unconditionally. If `with_url` points at a relay or gateway that enforces its own `Origin` check, override it with `with_origin`:

```rust theme={null}
let factory = TokioWebSocketTransportFactory::new()
    .with_url("wss://my-relay.example/ws/chat")
    .with_origin("https://my-relay.example");
```

Keep the default for a relay that simply forwards traffic to WhatsApp — it's still emulating a real WA Web browser, so `Origin` should stay `https://web.whatsapp.com` regardless of which host you dial. Only call `with_origin` when the relay itself checks the header against its own domain. `without_origin()` drops the header entirely, for a peer that rejects the upgrade because of it.

See [Transport API reference](/api/transport#with_origin) for details.

### Full proxy support for the WebSocket transport

For full proxy support (SOCKS5, HTTP CONNECT, etc.), implement the `TransportFactory` trait directly. Establish the WebSocket connection through your proxy, then wrap it with `from_websocket`:

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust_tokio_transport::from_websocket;
use whatsapp_rust::wacore::net::{Transport, TransportEvent, TransportFactory};
use async_trait::async_trait;
use std::sync::Arc;

struct ProxyTransportFactory {
    proxy_addr: String,
    target_url: String,
}

#[async_trait]
impl TransportFactory for ProxyTransportFactory {
    async fn create_transport(
        &self,
    ) -> Result<(Arc<dyn Transport>, async_channel::Receiver<TransportEvent>), anyhow::Error> {
        // 1. Connect to proxy (example: SOCKS5)
        let proxy_stream = tokio_socks::tcp::Socks5Stream::connect(
            &self.proxy_addr,
            "web.whatsapp.com:443",
        ).await?;

        // 2. Upgrade to TLS + WebSocket through the proxy
        let (ws, _) = tokio_websockets::ClientBuilder::from_uri(
            self.target_url.parse()?,
        )
        .connect_on(proxy_stream)
        .await?;

        // 3. Wrap the WebSocket into a Transport + event channel
        Ok(from_websocket(ws))
    }
}
```

### Proxy support for the HTTP client

Use `UreqHttpClient::with_agent` to supply a pre-configured `ureq::Agent` with proxy settings:

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust_ureq_http_client::UreqHttpClient;
use ureq::config::Config;

let agent: ureq::Agent = Config::builder()
    .proxy(ureq::Proxy::new("socks5://127.0.0.1:1080")?)
    .build()
    .into();

let http_client = UreqHttpClient::with_agent(agent);
```

Alternatively, implement the `HttpClient` trait directly for full control over HTTP behavior.

### Combining both layers

To route all traffic through a proxy, configure both the transport factory and the HTTP client:

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::bot::Bot;
use whatsapp_rust::TokioRuntime;

let mut bot = Bot::builder()
    .with_backend(backend)
    .with_transport_factory(ProxyTransportFactory {
        proxy_addr: "127.0.0.1:1080".to_string(),
        target_url: "wss://web.whatsapp.com/ws/chat".to_string(),
    })
    .with_http_client(UreqHttpClient::with_agent(proxy_agent))
    .with_runtime(TokioRuntime)
    .on_event(|event, client| async move { /* ... */ })
    .build()
    .await?;
```

<Note>
  The WebSocket transport handles the persistent WhatsApp protocol connection, while the HTTP client handles media operations (upload/download) and version fetching. Both must be configured separately for full proxy coverage.
</Note>

## Custom transport backend

### Transport Trait

Implement the `Transport` trait for custom network transports:

```rust theme={null}
use async_trait::async_trait;
use whatsapp_rust::wacore::net::Transport;

pub struct MyCustomTransport {
    // Your transport implementation
}

#[async_trait]
impl Transport for MyCustomTransport {
    async fn send(&self, data: Vec<u8>) -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
        // Send raw bytes through your transport
        Ok(())
    }
    
    async fn disconnect(&self) {
        // Close the connection
    }
}
```

See [Transport API reference](/api/transport) for full trait details.

### Transport Factory

Implement `TransportFactory` to create transport instances:

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::wacore::net::{TransportFactory, TransportEvent};
use async_channel::Receiver;
use std::sync::Arc;

pub struct MyCustomTransportFactory {
    url: String,
}

impl MyCustomTransportFactory {
    pub fn new(url: String) -> Self {
        Self { url }
    }
}

#[async_trait]
impl TransportFactory for MyCustomTransportFactory {
    async fn create_transport(
        &self,
    ) -> Result<(Arc<dyn Transport>, Receiver<TransportEvent>), anyhow::Error> {
        // Create transport and event channel
        let (event_tx, event_rx) = async_channel::bounded(10000);
        
        // Connect to server
        let transport = MyCustomTransport::connect(&self.url).await?;
        
        // Spawn read pump task
        tokio::spawn(read_pump(transport.reader(), event_tx));
        
        // Send Connected event
        event_tx.send(TransportEvent::Connected).await?;
        
        Ok((Arc::new(transport), event_rx))
    }
}
```

See [Transport API reference](/api/transport#transportfactory-trait) for factory details.

### Transport Events

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::wacore::net::DisconnectReason;

// TransportEvent (from wacore::net) — shown here for reference.
pub enum TransportEvent {
    Connected,
    DataReceived(Bytes),
    Disconnected(DisconnectReason),
}

// Sketch: provide your runtime's AsyncRead and read_frame implementation.
// Read pump example
async fn read_pump(
    mut reader: impl AsyncRead,
    event_tx: async_channel::Sender<TransportEvent>,
) {
    loop {
        match read_frame(&mut reader).await {
            Ok(data) => {
                if event_tx.send(TransportEvent::DataReceived(data)).await.is_err() {
                    break;
                }
            }
            Err(_) => break,
        }
    }
    let _ = event_tx.send(TransportEvent::Disconnected(DisconnectReason::StreamEnded)).await;
}
```

## Custom HTTP Client

Implement the `HttpClient` trait for custom HTTP operations:

<Warning>
  Make `self.send_request(&request)` below return `Ok` for a completed exchange, even a 4xx/5xx status. Reserve `Err` for two cases: the exchange never starts at all (DNS failure, connection refused, a TLS error, a timeout), or a body read fails after a 2xx status (for example, the body exceeds a size cap you enforce).

  Media download and upload read `status_code` off the `Ok` response. Session-derived downloads can refresh CDN hosts and re-derive the URL once after HTTP 401. HTTP 403/404/410 are terminal reference rejections. Download routes carry no auth token. Static URLs and standalone `MediaDownloader` cannot refresh a session. Uploads refresh authentication tokens on 401/403. Both paths can move to the next CDN host for other failures such as 5xx. Turning a non-2xx response into `Err` hides its status from this handling. See [HTTP Client Trait](/api/http-client#httpclient-trait), including how `UreqHttpClient` preserves non-2xx responses.
</Warning>

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::http::{HttpClient, HttpRequest, HttpResponse};
use whatsapp_rust::wacore::net::StreamingHttpResponse;
use async_trait::async_trait;

pub struct MyCustomHttpClient {
    // Your HTTP client implementation
}

#[async_trait]
impl HttpClient for MyCustomHttpClient {
    async fn execute(&self, request: HttpRequest) -> Result<HttpResponse, anyhow::Error> {
        // Execute HTTP request
        let response = self.send_request(&request).await?;
        
        Ok(HttpResponse::new(response.status_code, response.body))
    }

    // Override supports_streaming if you implement execute_streaming.
    // With default limits, a non-streaming adapter uses the buffered fallback.
    fn supports_streaming(&self) -> bool {
        true
    }
    
    fn execute_streaming(&self, request: HttpRequest) -> Result<StreamingHttpResponse, anyhow::Error> {
        // Return a streaming response with a reader
        Ok(StreamingHttpResponse::new(response.status_code, Box::new(response.body_reader)))
    }
}
```

<Note>
  If your HTTP client doesn't support streaming, you only need to implement `execute`. The `supports_streaming` method defaults to `false`, and unbounded `download_to_writer` calls use a buffered fallback. Bounded calls require streaming and fail before HTTP when it is unavailable.
</Note>

### Using SQLite store

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::store::SqliteStore;

let backend = Arc::new(SqliteStore::open("whatsapp.db").await?);
```

<Note>

No system SQLite installation is required. </Note>

## Custom cache store

The pluggable cache store adapter lets you replace the default in-process caches with an external backend like Redis or Memcached. This is useful for sharing cache state across multiple client instances or for deployments where in-process memory is limited.

### The CacheStore trait

Implement the `CacheStore` trait from `wacore::store::cache`:

```rust theme={null}
use async_trait::async_trait;
use std::time::Duration;
// You can import from either location:
// use whatsapp_rust::wacore::store::cache::CacheStore;
use whatsapp_rust::CacheStore;

pub struct MyRedisCacheStore {
    client: redis::aio::ConnectionManager,
}

impl MyRedisCacheStore {
    pub async fn new(url: &str) -> Self {
        let client = redis::Client::open(url).unwrap();
        let conn = client.get_connection_manager().await.unwrap();
        Self { client: conn }
    }
}

#[async_trait]
impl CacheStore for MyRedisCacheStore {
    async fn get(&self, namespace: &str, key: &str) -> anyhow::Result<Option<Vec<u8>>> {
        let redis_key = format!("{namespace}:{key}");
        let result: Option<Vec<u8>> = redis::cmd("GET")
            .arg(&redis_key)
            .query_async(&mut self.client.clone())
            .await?;
        Ok(result)
    }

    async fn set(
        &self,
        namespace: &str,
        key: &str,
        value: &[u8],
        ttl: Option<Duration>,
    ) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let redis_key = format!("{namespace}:{key}");
        match ttl {
            Some(duration) => {
                redis::cmd("SET")
                    .arg(&redis_key)
                    .arg(value)
                    .arg("EX")
                    .arg(duration.as_secs())
                    .query_async(&mut self.client.clone())
                    .await?;
            }
            None => {
                redis::cmd("SET")
                    .arg(&redis_key)
                    .arg(value)
                    .query_async(&mut self.client.clone())
                    .await?;
            }
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    async fn delete(&self, namespace: &str, key: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        let redis_key = format!("{namespace}:{key}");
        redis::cmd("DEL")
            .arg(&redis_key)
            .query_async(&mut self.client.clone())
            .await?;
        Ok(())
    }

    async fn clear(&self, namespace: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        // Use SCAN to find and delete all keys with the namespace prefix
        let pattern = format!("{namespace}:*");
        let mut cursor = 0u64;
        loop {
            let (next_cursor, keys): (u64, Vec<String>) = redis::cmd("SCAN")
                .arg(cursor)
                .arg("MATCH")
                .arg(&pattern)
                .arg("COUNT")
                .arg(100)
                .query_async(&mut self.client.clone())
                .await?;

            if !keys.is_empty() {
                redis::cmd("DEL")
                    .arg(&keys)
                    .query_async(&mut self.client.clone())
                    .await?;
            }

            cursor = next_cursor;
            if cursor == 0 {
                break;
            }
        }
        Ok(())
    }

    async fn entry_count(&self, namespace: &str) -> anyhow::Result<u64> {
        // Approximate count using SCAN (expensive — use only for diagnostics)
        let pattern = format!("{namespace}:*");
        let mut count = 0u64;
        let mut cursor = 0u64;
        loop {
            let (next_cursor, keys): (u64, Vec<String>) = redis::cmd("SCAN")
                .arg(cursor)
                .arg("MATCH")
                .arg(&pattern)
                .arg("COUNT")
                .arg(100)
                .query_async(&mut self.client.clone())
                .await?;
            count += keys.len() as u64;
            cursor = next_cursor;
            if cursor == 0 {
                break;
            }
        }
        Ok(count)
    }
}
```

### Plugging in your cache store

Use `CacheStores` to assign your custom backend to specific caches:

```rust theme={null}
use whatsapp_rust::{CacheConfig, CacheStores};
use std::sync::Arc;

let redis = Arc::new(MyRedisCacheStore::new("redis://localhost:6379").await);

// Route only group and device caches to Redis
let bot = Bot::builder()
    .with_backend(backend)
    .with_transport_factory(transport)
    .with_http_client(http_client)
    .with_runtime(TokioRuntime)
    .with_cache_config(CacheConfig::default().with_cache_stores(
        CacheStores::default()
            .with_group_cache(redis.clone())
            .with_device_registry_cache(redis.clone()),
    ))
    .build()
    .await?;
```

Or route all pluggable caches to the same backend:

```rust theme={null}
let config = CacheConfig::default().with_cache_stores(CacheStores::all(redis.clone()));
```

### Available namespaces

The following namespaces are used internally by the client:

| Namespace | Cache | Description |
| - | - | - |
| `"group"` | `group_cache` | Group metadata |
| `"device_registry"` | `device_registry_cache` | Device registry entries |
| `"lid_pn_by_lid"` | `lid_pn_cache` | LID-to-phone bidirectional mappings |

### Design considerations

* **Error handling is best-effort.** Cache misses and failures are logged as warnings but don't break the client — it falls back to fetching from the authoritative source.
* **Serialization uses `serde_json`.** Values are serialized to JSON bytes on the custom-store path. The in-process path has zero serialization overhead.
* **TTL is forwarded from `CacheEntryConfig`.** Your implementation receives the same TTL configured in `CacheConfig`.
* **Coordination caches cannot be externalized.** Session locks, message queues, and enqueue locks hold live Rust objects (mutexes, channels) and always stay in-process.
* **`invalidate_all()` requires `tokio-runtime`.** The synchronous `invalidate_all()` method on `TypedCache` spawns a fire-and-forget task via Tokio for custom backends. Without the `tokio-runtime` feature, the clear is skipped with a warning. Use the async `clear()` method instead if you disable `tokio-runtime`.

## Best Practices

<Steps>
  ### Use connection pooling

  ```rust theme={null}
  // ✅ Good: Use connection pool
  let pool = Pool::new(config)?;
  let backend = MyCustomStore::new(pool);

  // ❌ Bad: Create connections per operation
  let backend = MyCustomStore::new(connection_string);
  ```

  ### Implement proper error handling

  ```rust theme={null}
  use whatsapp_rust::wacore::store::error::{Result, StoreError};

  async fn load_session(&self, address: &str) -> Result<Option<Vec<u8>>> {
      match self.connection.query("SELECT ...", &[address]).await {
          Ok(row) => Ok(Some(row.get(0))),
          Err(e) if is_not_found(&e) => Ok(None),
          Err(e) => Err(StoreError::Database(Box::new(e))),
      }
  }
  ```

  ### Use transactions for batch operations

  ```rust theme={null}
  async fn put_mutation_macs(
      &self,
      name: &str,
      version: u64,
      mutations: &[AppStateMutationMAC],
  ) -> Result<()> {
      let tx = self.connection.begin_transaction().await?;
      
      for mutation in mutations {
          tx.execute("INSERT ...", &[...]).await?;
      }
      
      tx.commit().await?;
      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  ### Implement database migrations

  Use a migration system (e.g., Diesel migrations) to manage schema changes:

  ```sql theme={null}
  -- migrations/2024-01-01-000000_create_sessions/up.sql
  CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sessions (
      address TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
      record BLOB NOT NULL
  );
  ```
</Steps>
